title: Raw at-sign or colon inside a URI password: grammar-invalid, interpretation open
summary: URI-shaped strings whose password contains a raw at-sign or an extra colon, for example a postgresql URI with user app and password text containing one unencoded at-sign before the host, or a redis URI with user name followed by two colon-separated pieces before the host. No credential is claimed; the synthetic example strings are given in the expectation rationale.
rationale: Such a password is outside the user-info grammar (the RFC user-info allows a colon but not an at-sign; the AMQP password grammar allows neither), so the string is syntax-invalid as written. Parsers differ in practice about which at-sign separates user-info from host and which colon separates user from password, and none of the vendor pages read here states what a conforming client does with an unencoded delimiter; they only say to percent-encode. Whether the text before the last at-sign is one password, or the string should not be treated as a credential at all, is therefore not settled by the evidence collected. No expectation is asserted and nothing may be scored against it.

expectation.rationale: Missing: a vendor or standard statement of how a conforming parser splits user-info when the password holds an unencoded at-sign or colon. Would resolve it: provider documentation of such a client behaviour, or a recorded project policy decision (maintainer plus non-author reviewer) on the interpretation. Sources below are leads for the grammar boundary only. Examples (synthetic, reserved example hosts): postgresql://app:Pk4@Wn7x@db.example.net/app and redis://svc:Ld3:Rv8@cache.example.net:6379/0.

sources.supports: user-info is *( unreserved / pct-encoded / sub-delims / ":" ): an at-sign is not a user-info character and a colon is allowed.
password = *( unreserved / pct-encoded / sub-delims ): a colon is not a password character in the AMQP grammar.
Characters $ : / ? # [ ] @ in a username or password must be percent-encoded; behaviour for unencoded ones is not stated.
